newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Shaba copperbelt hopes for post-war boom.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Shaba copperbelt hopes for post-war boom.

text.p: The people of Shaba province, whose mineral wealth has helped keep President Mobutu Sese Seko's Zaire afloat during three decades of chaos and decline, have high hopes of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
Ordinary people complain that corruption and self-enrichment by officials have eaten away at hopes of economic progress.
"He must go away, that crazy crook president," a waiter in a city centre cafe commented bitterly.
The region, better known locally by its traditional name Katanga, is sitting on some of the world's richest reserves of copper, cobalt and other precious minerals.
Previous challenges to Mobutu's rule have failed but now rebels under Laurent Kabila, himself a Katangan, are putting up the most serious challenge to his rule to date.
With Mobutu, 66, weak from cancer treatment, Kabila's forces control one fifth of Zaire and say they are 200 km (125 miles) from Shaba's capital Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city.
Residents eagerly await their arrival.

They swap the tales they have heard of a better life in the rebel-held east of the country, where they say the rule of law has been imposed, corrupt police and officials get their deserved rebuke or punishment and money and wages once again have real worth.

Sociology student Assani Mandevu, born in 1965, the year Mobutu seized power, hopes for a brighter future. "I want him (Mubutu) to see the rebels take power by force and watch what a good job they do of running the country he has ruined," he said.
The prospect of a new government has come at a time when political changes across southern Africa and new economic realities are giving Shaba's economy fresh hope.

Two decades after nationalisation, state-owned Gecamines, which controls Shaba's mines and its economy, has embarked on a programme of privatisation that late last year attracted the first major foreign investments to Zaire since the 1970s.
South African, Belgian or British mine experts in Lubumbashi not expect the war to jeopardise their investments long term.
South Africa's emergence from the isolation of apartheid has turned it into the regional power on which Shaba and the whole region depend for future trade and success.
As close to Johannesburg as it is to the capital Kinshasa, Lubumbashi already looks south more than it looks north or west.
"Practically no goods arrive here from Kinshasa any more," says Patrick Claes of the South African-Belgian railways company Sizarail that has got goods moving again in southeast Zaire.
The shops are full of South African goods that his railway brings into the country along with the coal and other supplies the mines need. The trains take the copper and cobalt out.
Geographically, Shaba, the size of France, is more southern than central African, with a dry climate and bush plains.
Kinshasa is 1,700 km (1,050 miles) of jungle away as the crow flies. Transport by rail and river is slow and difficult. Reaching Zaire's Atlantic port at Matadi, can take weeks.
Shaba has regularly tried to fight its way out of Zaire since the Belgian Congo won independence in 1960.
Memories of a 1978 massacre by Katangan separatists of Belgians in the copper mining town of Kolwezi, still sends a shiver down expatriate spines here in times of trouble.
Shabans resent the flow of the province's wealth to Kinshasa or into the pockets of officials on the way. They want change.
This time, however, local leaders shun talk of seccession. What they want is autonomy -- in the form of confederation.
